segments.source: Four plots lie in a line A–B–C–D. Assign one different use to each plot: school, factory, park, homes. Constraints: the factory may not be adjacent to the school; the park must be adjacent to the homes. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 9 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.
Rules.
An assignment is valid only if every use is placed exactly once and all adjacency constraints hold. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.
Task.
Give one valid assignment and explain why it satisfies every constraint. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Try the assignment A=factory, B=park, C=homes, D=school. 2. Factory and school are not adjacent. 3. Park and homes are adjacent. 4. Each use appears exactly once. Cross-domain check: 9−4=5 independent reports remain.
Answer.
A=factory, B=park, C=homes, D=school is a valid assignment. Cross-domain answer: 5 independent reports.
Knowledge takeaway.
A place can be unsuitable not because of its own properties, but because of what would be next to it.
Formal model.
Permutation CSP with all-different and adjacency/non-adjacency constraints.
Problem 404. Land-use compatibility on four plots: case 4
Knowledge context.
Land-use planning combines spatial relationships with compatibility rules.
Given facts.

Four plots lie in a line A–B–C–D. Assign one different use to each plot: school, factory, park, homes. Constraints: the factory may not be adjacent to the school; the park must be adjacent to the homes. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 6 km and two checkpoints are 7 cm apart.
Rules.
An assignment is valid only if every use is placed exactly once and all adjacency constraints hold. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.
Task.
Give one valid assignment and explain why it satisfies every constraint. Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?
Step-by-step solution.
1. Try the assignment A=factory, B=homes, C=park, D=school. 2. Factory and school are not adjacent. 3. Park and homes are adjacent. 4. Each use appears exactly once. Cross-domain check: 7×6=42 km.
Answer.
A=factory, B=homes, C=park, D=school is a valid assignment. Cross-domain answer: 42 km.
Knowledge takeaway.
A place can be unsuitable not because of its own properties, but because of what would be next to it.
Formal model.
Permutation CSP with all-different and adjacency/non-adjacency constraints.
Problem 405. Land-use compatibility on four plots: case 5
Knowledge context.
Land-use planning combines spatial relationships with compatibility rules.
Given facts.

Four plots lie in a line A–B–C–D. Assign one different use to each plot: school, factory, park, homes. Constraints: the factory may not be adjacent to the school; the park must be adjacent to the homes. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.
Rules.
An assignment is valid only if every use is placed exactly once and all adjacency constraints hold. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.
Task.
Give one valid assignment and explain why it satisfies every constraint. Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Try the assignment A=school, B=park, C=homes, D=factory. 2. Factory and school are not adjacent. 3. Park and homes are adjacent. 4. Each use appears exactly once. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00.
Answer.
A=school, B=park, C=homes, D=factory is a valid assignment. Cross-domain answer: 14:00.
Knowledge takeaway.
A place can be unsuitable not because of its own properties, but because of what would be next to it.
Formal model.
Permutation CSP with all-different and adjacency/non-adjacency constraints.
N7. Natural risk: hazard, exposure, protection
Problem 406. Hazard, exposure, and protection: case 1
Knowledge context.
Natural risk depends on more than the physical hazard. Exposure and protective measures also affect outcomes.
Given facts.

For this classroom model, risk index = hazard × exposure ÷ protection. Data: Site A: hazard=2, exposure=4, protection=1; Site B: hazard=4, exposure=2, protection=2; Site C: hazard=3, exposure=3, protection=2.
Rules.
Use the formula exactly as stated. A higher hazard does not necessarily mean higher risk if exposure or protection differs.
Task.
Compute the risk index for each site. Which site has the lowest modeled risk?
Step-by-step solution.
